title: How Zero Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the history and mathematical oddities of zero. They trace its origins from Sumerian placeholder marks on clay tablets, through Babylonian positional notation, Roman numerals' lack of zero, its conception as a number in fifth-century India (attributed to Aryabhata, as Josh is corrected to "discovered" or "created"), its transmission to the West via Arabs and Fibonacci, independent Maya use for calendars, the missing year zero in the Gregorian calendar and Cassini's astronomical numbering, zero's role in the decimal system and fractions, its arithmetic properties (additive identity, additive inverse, multiplication, division by zero, zero exponent), and elevator floor numbering in countries once ruled by the Ottomans. The episode closes with a South by Southwest live show announcement and a listener mail about coffee and a coffee song.
topics: Robert Kaplan The Nothing That Is

segments.title: Opening banter and zero's many facets
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck introduce the episode as a non-math-heavy history of zero, joking about its many facets and its name across languages (nol, cero, zilch, sunya, sifr, zephyrum, zero).

segments.title: Zero as placeholder in Sumerian and Babylonian numerals
segments.summary: The hosts describe Sumerian clay tablets using wedges and hooks as placeholders so that numbers like 3000 and 300 can be distinguished, and how the Babylonians' positional system made zero necessary. Kaplan's speculation about the origin of the heavy dot symbol is mentioned.
topics: Robert Kaplan The Nothing That Is

segments.title: Fear of zero and Roman numerals
segments.summary: Discussion of why zero was uneasy for some cultures, associated with void and chaos, and how the Romans lacked zero in their numeral system, with the word nulla used without a numeral symbol.

segments.title: Zero as a number in India and transmission to the West
segments.summary: Zero's conception as a number is attributed to fifth-century India, possibly to Aryabhata. Arab nations spread it, and Fibonacci, son of a customs officer in Algeria, learned Arabic numerals from Arabic tutors and introduced them to the West through his book.

segments.title: Maya zero and calendar counting
segments.summary: The Maya independently used zero as a base for counting, mainly for their calendar, with day zero followed by one, two, three. The hosts note the Gregorian calendar has no year zero.

segments.title: Year zero, Cassini and the number line
segments.summary: Western astronomers, credited to Jacques Cassini, designated 1 BC as year zero, with negative and positive years on either side. Zero is described as the fulcrum between positive and negative numbers and as a whole integer.

segments.title: Decimal system, fractions and precision
segments.summary: Zero enables the decimal system and fractions, allowing precise measurement such as machine parts and small quantities, which whole numbers alone could not do.

segments.title: Properties of zero: addition, multiplication, division, exponents
segments.summary: The hosts cover the additive identity, additive inverses, multiplication by zero, why division by zero is undefined with the six divided by zero example, Stephen Hawking's joke about black holes, and the zero exponent equaling one.

segments.title: Elevator floor numbering in formerly Ottoman lands
segments.summary: Elevators in Hungary and Spain, once ruled by the Ottoman Turks, label the ground floor zero with basements as negative numbers, cited as evidence of comfort with zero.

segments.title: Show announcement: South by Southwest live show
segments.summary: Josh announces a live podcast at South by Southwest in Austin, Texas on March 11, 2012, plus a Monday party for non-badge holders.

segments.title: Listener mail: coffee and the coffee song
segments.summary: Listener Ashley from Edmonton, Alberta writes about coffee blends at cafes and Starbucks, and sends a coffee song, which is played.
